finding.public_domain_rationale: The work was first published in 1924 as a two-piano score. Under the U.S. term for works published before 1978, the 95-year published-work term places the 1924 composition/edition in the public domain on January 1, 2020. This answer is limited to the underlying 1924 Gershwin composition/edition: a later arrangement, notably Grofe's 1942 orchestration, is a separate copyright question, and a sound recording is a separate neighboring-rights question. The identified 1924 recording is separately reported as U.S. public domain from January 1, 2025, but that does not identify the master used in the cut or resolve non-U.S. rights.
finding.territory_notes: The original 1924 Gershwin composition/edition is out of copyright in the United States, but that conclusion does not automatically cover an arrangement or a recording worldwide. The research source lists the 1924 Jazz Band and 1926 Theatre Orchestra settings as public domain in the USA but not Canada. It separately states that the 1942 Ferde Grofe symphonic orchestration remains protected in the USA until January 1, 2038 and is not public domain in Canada/EU. For Nightshift's worldwide, all-media, in-perpetuity use, identify the exact edition/arrangement and recording and obtain territory-specific confirmation; no complete country-by-country determination was found.
finding.licensing_precedent: Documented screen uses include the Gershwin composition in the soundtrack of Manhattan, and Fantasia 2000's use of an edited Grofe orchestration performed by the Philharmonia Orchestra conducted by Bruce Broughton. A 1945 Rhapsody in Blue film also used Gershwin material with Grofe orchestration. No reported fee for any of those uses, and no Rhapsody-specific fee for a worldwide, all-media, perpetual featured-film placement, was found. Generic market guidance located during research is not a reliable quote for this use: it gave examples ranging from about $250 for background television use to $250,000-plus for a national U.S. commercial and high-six-figure global campaigns, rather than a work-specific film licence.
unresolved: The exact master in the cut is not identified: no supplied recording file, performer, ISRC, label/catalogue number, release date, or other identifier. The audible clarinet glissando is consistent with the Library of Congress description of the June 10, 1924 Whiteman/Gershwin recording, but that does not prove it is the recording used in Nightshift.

If the candidate is the 1924 Victor acoustic release, public sources establish the historical Victor release but do not trace the assignment/succession from Victor to a current legal master owner or provide a current licensing contact. Do not infer Sony or another current label as owner without a recording-specific catalogue/chain document.

entries.outreach_draft:
Dear A Gershwin, LLC,

We are writing on behalf of the production "Nightshift" to request rights clearance for the musical work "Rhapsody in Blue (1924)."

The material appears in the film's rough cut (v4) from timecode 0:14:22 to 0:15:31, for an approximate duration of 1 minute and 9 seconds. During this scene, the piece plays on a diner's radio while the character Mara counts the till.

We are seeking rights for worldwide territory, across all media, in perpetuity.

Please note that the composition and the sound recording may be controlled separately. Kindly advise if you control only one side of these rights.

We are seeking a synchronisation licence for the composition. We also require a master use licence for the specific sound recording used in the film. The exact master recording has not been identified. While the audible clarinet glissando is consistent with the Library of Congress description of the June 10, 1924 Whiteman/Gershwin recording, we do not have definitive confirmation that this is the recording used. Furthermore, public sources do not provide a clear chain of title from the historical Victor release to a current legal master owner or a current licensing contact. Please advise if you can provide guidance on the current owner of the master recording for this work, or if you control rights to a master recording that matches the description.

Please confirm your ability to grant these rights, your licensing fee, and any restrictions that may apply.

Dear The Coca-Cola Company,

We are writing on behalf of the production "Nightshift" (rough cut v4) to request clearance for the use of the Coca-Cola trademark.

The material appears from 0:45:11 to 0:45:29, for approximately 18 seconds. In the scene, a vending machine fills the frame. A character named Dov kicks the machine, and the Coca-Cola logo is visible centre-frame as the machine topples. The trademark is prominently featured.

We are seeking a trademark usage release for worldwide territory, in perpetuity, across all media.

We have not yet identified the specific trademark registration(s) covering the contour-bottle silhouette, red spot/color treatment, and any partially obscured can label by registration number or jurisdiction. Additionally, the precise territorial ownership or control split between The Coca-Cola Company and its subsidiaries for a worldwide license has not been established. We would appreciate any guidance you can offer regarding these points.

Please confirm your ability to grant these rights, your fee for such use, and any restrictions or conditions that may apply.

With the choice of _Starry Night,_ the work appeals to both Oh, as it depicts the Milky Way, and Tip as it depicts the yearning for home. This really touches upon us as the audience, as we relate to their struggles and desires, but also provides an Easter egg for those of us who are art history lovers. Just as Oh the alien wants somewhere to belong and Tip wants the security of her mother, in reality van Gogh had those same yearnings. > Van Gogh, who was ostracized by many communities during his lifetime, moved frequently searching for a home. > > He wanted somewhere to belong and sought companionship through the form of consorts and lovers. He relied heavily on his brother and sister-in-law for support, often making for strained relations. Van Gogh wanted more in his life and unfortunately never found that longed for commercial success or personal fulfillment in his lifetime. However we revere him today as a master at his craft, and in the movie well I wont spoil that for you but for those of you haven’t seen it you should.
